voiceNote: One narrator for every clip. Generated once with scripts/generate-narration.mjs; see docs/NARRATION.md.

items.title: Welcome
items.text: Welcome aboard. Your lunar journey begins now.

items.title: The Moon and its south pole
items.text: This is the Moon, shown with imagery from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. Near the south pole the Sun never climbs far above the horizon, so long shadows shape the landscape. Some crater floors here never receive direct sunlight, and they are cold enough to hold water ice. Nearby rims and peaks, by contrast, can stay sunlit for much of the year. NASA has named nine candidate regions for the Artemis Three landing. This app measures, from real terrain data, when each of them can see the Sun and the Earth.

items.title: Peak near Cabeus B
items.text: Peak near Cabeus B is a candidate region on high ground near the crater Cabeus B, about eighty-four degrees south. Its neighbour, the crater Cabeus, is where NASA's LCROSS mission struck the Moon in 2009 and detected water in the material it threw up. At the observation point this app uses inside NASA's outline, the centre of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-eight percent of 2027.

items.title: Haworth
items.text: The Haworth region lies on terrain beside Haworth crater, about fifty-one kilometres across, whose floor is permanently shadowed. At roughly thirty kilometres across, its outline is one of the larger ones NASA has drawn. At the observation point this app uses, the centre of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-six percent of 2027.

items.title: Malapert Massif
items.text: Malapert Massif is part of Mons Malapert, a broad mountain about sixty-seven kilometres across, named after the seventeenth-century astronomer Charles Malapert. It sits on the Earth-facing side of the south pole, so from its high ground the Earth is often above the horizon. At the observation point this app uses, the centre of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about sixty-three percent of 2027.

items.title: Mons Mouton Plateau
items.text: Mons Mouton Plateau is the largest of the nine outlines, roughly seventy-eight by fifty-eight kilometres, across the high and comparatively flat top of Mons Mouton. The mountain is named after Melba Roy Mouton, a NASA mathematician and programmer. At the observation point this app uses, the centre of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-five percent of 2027.

items.title: Mons Mouton
items.text: The Mons Mouton region is a smaller outline on the same mountain, on its slopes to the west of the large crater Nobile. Its high ground gives long views over the surrounding terrain. At the observation point this app uses, the centre of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about sixty-seven percent of 2027, the highest share among the nine points.

items.title: Nobile Rim 1
items.text: Nobile Rim One lies on the western rim of Nobile, a crater about seventy-nine kilometres across, named after the Italian polar explorer Umberto Nobile. Crater rims near the pole rise into sunlight while the crater floor stays in shadow. At the observation point this app uses, the centre of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about sixty-four percent of 2027.

items.title: Nobile Rim 2
items.text: Nobile Rim Two lies on the northern side of the same crater, Nobile, farther from the pole than Rim One. At the observation point this app uses, the centre of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-one percent of 2027, the lowest share among the nine points.

items.title: de Gerlache Rim 2
items.text: de Gerlache Rim Two is on the rim of de Gerlache, a crater about thirty-three kilometres across, named after the Belgian polar explorer Adrien de Gerlache. At about eighty-eight degrees south, it is the closest of the nine regions to the pole. At the observation point this app uses, the centre of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-eight percent of 2027.

items.title: Slater Plain
items.text: Slater Plain is a comparatively smooth area near Slater crater, about twenty-five kilometres across, named after the planetary scientist David Slater. It lies on the side of the pole facing away from the Earth's usual direction, so the Earth is often close to its horizon. At the observation point this app uses, the centre of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about sixty-two percent of 2027.

items.title: Standing on the surface
items.text: You are standing at the observation point, two metres above the ground. The terrain all the way to the horizon is built from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter measurements, so the skyline you see is the measured skyline. The Sun and the Earth are drawn at their true directions and sizes. The fine ground texture, the lifted shadows and the soft glow around the Sun and the Earth are display aids, not measurements. You can switch them off in the layers menu.

items.title: Reading Mission Analysis
items.text: Mission Analysis compares two places over a period you choose. Sun above the skyline is the share of time the centre of the Sun is visible, which matters for solar power and warmth. Earth above the skyline is the share of time the Earth is in geometric line of sight. That is needed for direct communication, but it does not guarantee a working link. The longest stretch without Sun shows how long equipment would have to last in darkness. Every result applies to one observation point, and slopes, hazards and operations are not modelled.

items.title: Elevation
items.text: Elevation is the angle of an object above the local horizontal plane. Zero degrees is level with the eye, and ninety degrees is straight overhead. Near the south pole the Sun's elevation stays within a few degrees of the horizon all year.

items.title: Azimuth
items.text: Azimuth is the compass direction of an object, measured clockwise from local north, which points toward the Moon's north pole. East is ninety degrees, south is one hundred and eighty, and west is two hundred and seventy.

items.title: Terrain skyline
items.text: The terrain skyline is the highest angle of the surrounding ground in a given direction. Here it is traced through NASA's LOLA elevation data out to one hundred and fifty kilometres. A body is hidden whenever its elevation is below the skyline, even if it is above the horizontal.

items.title: Clearance
items.text: Clearance is a body's elevation minus the skyline in its direction. A positive value means the centre of the Sun or the Earth is above the terrain. A negative value means the terrain hides it.

items.title: Observation coordinates
items.text: The coordinates give the observation point's latitude and longitude on the Moon, with east counted positive. The point is chosen by a fixed rule inside NASA's region outline. It is a representative point for these calculations, not a NASA landing site.

items.title: Visibility intervals
items.text: A visibility interval is a period in which a body stays above the skyline without interruption. The timelines draw them as bars. The longest gap without the Sun shows how long a landed system would face darkness.

items.title: Guided tour · 1 of 5
items.text: This is the Moon, as NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has mapped it. You can drag to turn it and scroll to zoom at any point in this tour.

items.title: Guided tour · 2 of 5
items.text: We are now above the lunar south pole. Here the Sun skims the horizon, so high ground can stay sunlit while deep craters stay dark. The outlines mark NASA's nine candidate regions for Artemis Three.

items.title: Guided tour · 3 of 5
items.text: This is Malapert Massif, one of the nine regions. The dot marks the point this app uses for its measurements. The panel on the right tells you whether the Sun and the Earth are visible from there at the selected time.

items.title: Guided tour · 4 of 5
items.text: Now we stand on the surface. The skyline is measured terrain. The strip at the bottom shows the whole horizon, with the Sun and the Earth marked. Drag to look around.

items.title: Guided tour · 5 of 5
items.text: Finally, Mission Analysis compares two regions over time: how often the Sun and the Earth are visible, and how long the darkness lasts. This is where you can weigh one site against another.
